topics.title: Introduction
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 1 - Introduction.txt

blocks.text: In simple terms, Exercise Science studies how physical activity affects the human body. This has become an increasingly important field in recent years due to the growing public awareness of the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle. And one of the most beneficial areas of study within Exercise Science is strength training, which involves using resistance to build muscular strength and endurance.

At MaxStrength Fitness, we specialize in strength training using a unique approach that emphasizes mechanical tension (MT) and progressive overload. Mechanical tension is the pulling force experienced by the active muscle fibers during physical activity and is physiologically required for stimulating hypertrophy and strength gains. Progressive overload refers to the gradually increasing capacity of a workout that are evidenced by and a result of an increase in strength. With a stronger muscle, a higher level of mechanical tension is now permitted and required to stimulate further strength gains. Although a consistently similar effort without necessarily increasing has proven to be enough to maintain strength, it's desirable to attempt to continuously train harder to optimize results. So our immediate goal of any workout would be to increase the number of motor units we are activating, which is known as Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR). The more motor units we can recruit through higher levels of effort, the more muscle fibers we are stimulating, thereby increasing the potential benefits of the exercise.

We create this mechanical tension, or muscular loading, using a highly focused movement protocol performed on specially designed resistance training equipment that properly tracks muscle and joint function. This equipment, along with our protocol and expert instruction, allows us to precisely target specific movement patterns, which, in turn, target specific muscle fibers and ensures the resistance is applied safely and effectively.

Our uniquely developed protocol, known as the MSF Continuous Tension method, takes full advantage of our equipment and leverages the current understanding of the mechanisms that create meaningful muscular tension. The cornerstone of our Continuous Tension method is a relatively slow and continuous speed of movement. We utilize a window of 6 to 10 seconds to lift (concentric) and 6 to 10 seconds to lower (eccentric) the resistance on every exercise. Of even greater importance is the careful and continuous change of direction between the eccentric and concentric phases of the movement. This exaggerated control reduces the momentum and sudden forces instinctively used by most trainees, simultaneously reducing the risks and increasing the effectiveness of lifting weights. A common expression used at MSF is that our protocol is designed to make exercise harder AND safer.

topics.title: Progressive Overload and Intensity
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 2 - Progressive Overload and Intensity.txt

blocks.text: Progressive Overload (PO) is the demonstration or evidence of an increase in strength performance as a result of the improvement of the physiological mechanisms responsible for strength increases. More simply stated, it is something we've achieved in this workout that we could not have done in the previous workout. It will only be apparent in one or two ways. Either using more load for the same number of reps or more reps with the same load. Both conditions would also require at least consistent form/quality or better. Completing a rep with poor form or using momentum or any number of discrepancies cannot be used to confidently substantiate that a strength gain has taken place. More importantly this approach to training is likely to deteriorate over time and carries with it a heightened risk of injury both acute and long-term.

The commonly held belief about Progressive Overload is that it is something that is "ensured" or forced by lifting more weight or performing more reps in each successive workout. Some trainers and influencers even suggest that you will achieve PO by adding more sets (increasing volume). But none of these suggestions are true. None of these actions will ensure a strength gain. Remember PO is the ability to do something that wasn't possible before. It is made possible as a result of a strength gain. And adding more sets only requires more time not more strength.

It is imperative that every MSF Exercise Practitioner clearly understand the specifics of these commonly used industry terms. Even more importantly, we should understand how to apply these concepts in the context of our methodology. In the case of PO, we need to first understand HOW it happens. Physiologically speaking, PO is the result of an increase in strength. Strength, however, is not an adaptation itself but rather an outcome of multiple adaptations. Most notably:
Increase in Motor Unit Recruitment (MUR)
Improved coordination and skill
Decreased coactivation of antagonists
Hypertrophy

topics.title: Progression - The Mastery of Effort
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 3 - Progression - The Mastery of Effort.txt

blocks.text: As the body adapts by becoming stronger and thus more capable and fit, it requires a more physically challenging stimulus in order to continue to improve. This progressive challenge does not automatically come about with more weight or sets or reps. In other words, more volume, or performing more of something does not create a greater degree of mechanical tension. Additionally, lifting more weight does not necessarily create more mechanical tension or an increased internal stimulus. Oftentimes a trainee will alter their form or use momentum or other discrepancies to lift more weight. As you will learn throughout this manual, more tension also comes about through a qualitatively optimized, more efficient, more focused, more volitionally directed effort. In other words, a more intense effort with greater control usually equates to a greater internal stimulus. [Keep in mind that mechanical tension, muscular tension, and internal stimulus are synonymous as used throughout this manual].

This qualitative effort is the single most important factor that one should look to progress when strength training. It is also not something that should be expected to come quickly or naturally. On the contrary, this ability will need to be practiced and developed over months and years. This should be viewed as a positive attribute in that it ensures a sustainably long potential for progress and adaptation across a multitude of variables. And this is really where the instructor should continue to steer the clients' focus over time. The instructor's ability to help the client conceptualize this then becomes a critical tool in retention. We are not basing our protocol or the client's success on quantitative elements but rather the mastery of their effort.

It is important to note here that this idea of "progress" is one of the more critical concepts that an Exercise Practitioner needs to be able to interpret, convey, and cultivate to and among our client base. The instructor and client need to understand that the load being lifted is the last variable of progression to be advanced. The execution of every inch of every exercise should be the primary focus of every workout. In other words, get better at training hard. And this is best accomplished by intently following the Exercise Practitioner's instruction.

If one were to simply improve the actual performance of an exercise by controlling their speed, changes of direction, breathing, demeanor, focus, timing of effort, etc., all while keeping the same load, they would most likely be creating more mechanical tension, thus creating a stimulus for growth. So by exaggerating one's control over the movements and looking to make that the priority in every workout, they not only create a stimulus but they make the workouts safer as well.

One last note on mastering progression in training…the real limiter to continued progress is one’s maximum tolerable perception of effort. Basically how difficult or even threatening each subject perceives their current level of effort. Once the maximum level is reached, the brain will not recruit any more motor units (muscle fibers) and the exercise movement will cease. Importantly, this maximum level of perceived effort can increase over time and the best way to go about improving here is simply by training more. Simply stated, training more will help a subject tolerate higher levels of effort. This is great news for anyone looking to continue to make progress and is the primary reason our clients should remain clients for the rest of their lives!

topics.title: Volume
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 4 - Volume.txt

blocks.text: Training volume can be measured in many ways but most commonly refers to the amount of work performed during a training session, usually consisting of the total number of sets and reps in a workout. Importantly, there is an inverse relationship between intensity of effort and volume of work or exercise that can be performed. The higher the intensity of a set of exercise, the lower the volume a person can perform, tolerate, and recover from. Furthermore, as the volume in a singular workout increases, the effect or benefit of the subsequent sets and exercises decreases. This is due to both central nervous system fatigue as well as peripheral fatigue experienced locally by the working muscles. The accumulating fatigue causes an interference as a protective mechanism in the form of reduced motor unit recruitment and mechanical tension; the two physiological characteristics required for a hypertrophic stimulus.

The research comparing the effectiveness of varying volume per exercise shows no significant difference between performing one, two, three, or more sets for the majority of trainees, and empirical evidence suggests fewer sets are more effective at higher levels of intensity as discussed above. And if performed properly, more than two sets of any given exercise would not be desirable by most or even possible for some of the more advanced trainees. This is why only one set per exercise is performed utilizing our Continuous Tension method. We will discuss the specific situations a client may perform more than one set later in the module.

To keep the overall workout volume low, and therefore improve the ability to maintain a high intensity, the number of exercises should be limited to the least required. Each workout (or workout rotation) should effectively address all of the major muscle groups and any smaller muscle groups important to the trainee's goals, without accumulating what is known as "junk volume". For a majority of subjects, this will be between 5 to 8 exercises total, with the higher number of exercises usually reserved for more advanced trainees and consisting of several smaller, less systemically demanding movements.

It is also important to note here that many novice or inexperienced trainees will feel the need to perform more exercises as they will most certainly (and incorrectly) believe that more exercise is better. This seems to be the universal belief of the majority about exercise. It is imperative that the Exercise Practitioner continually educate the client that it is NOT volume or the number of exercises that drives the physiological benefits we seek but rather the intensity of their effort. Again, bring their attention back to the quality of their execution, the mastery and tolerance of their effort.

Novice trainees are unlikely to have the ability or focus to truly create a high-intensity effort but that alone does not preclude the exercise from being beneficial. The requirement for a productive stimulus is significantly lower in an untrained or novice subject, and oftentimes the slightest amount of controlled exertion will be novel enough to suffice. But as the subject gains experience and exposes themselves to more and more stimulus (training), the intensity of effort becomes paramount. This concept needs to be emphasized by the trainer and made the primary point of focus as the client progresses over their training life. Again, it is the intensity of the effort that produces the stimulus for change, not the volume or "amount" of exercise.

topics.title: Frequency
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 5 - Frequency.txt

blocks.text: Why Frequency Matters

Exercise produces its benefits through adaptation. Each training session creates a certain degree of stimulus and fatigue. Ideally, the stimulus would be maximized and the fatigue minimized, resulting in a net benefit or stimulus. For this adaptive process to occur optimally, sufficient time must be allowed between workouts for fatigue to dissipate. When residual fatigue remains, the effectiveness of subsequent training sessions is compromised.

Recovery timelines vary across physiological systems and between individuals. Factors such as recent training volume, age, genetics, nutrition, stress, and sleep quality all influence how quickly a person recovers. Training too frequently, beyond one’s capacity to recover, increases the risk of overtraining, overuse injuries, and stalled progress. Conversely, training too infrequently fails to provide a consistent enough signal for the body to maintain or improve its adaptations.
What the Research Supports

The majority of exercise research supports training the entire body two, and at most three, times per week. When total weekly training volume is equalized, research shows little difference in outcomes between two or three weekly sessions. In addition to this, the period of elevated myofibrillar protein synthesis (MYOPS) that results from a high intensity workout tends to last somewhere between 48 to 72 hours. This is where protein in the form of nutrients are synthesized by the body to create new contractile tissue, or muscle. Once we exit this elevated period, it would be ideal to train again to stimulate the elevated MYOPS. As a result, two full-body workouts per week represent the most efficient and conservative recommendation for the majority of trainees, assuming fatigue is properly managed.

This frequency balances stimulus and recovery while minimizing unnecessary fatigue and time commitment. It also aligns well with long-term sustainability, which is essential for lifelong strength training adherence.
Muscle Fiber Specificity and Frequency

Hypertrophy and strength adaptations are muscle fiber specific. Only the muscle fibers that are recruited and exposed to sufficient mechanical tension will adapt. As a result, training frequency only produces benefits when the same muscle fibers are repeatedly stimulated across workouts.

This highlights an often-missed point. Frequency alone does not drive progress. Repeated stimulation of the same muscle fibers does. Performing two workouts per week is only advantageous if there is meaningful overlap in the muscle fibers being trained during each session.
Managing Variety Without Compromising Results

Human nature favors novelty, and this tendency is especially evident in clients who desire constant variety in their workouts. Left unchecked, this preference would result in entirely different exercises every session. While this may feel engaging, it undermines the benefit of training frequency and slows progress by dispersing the stimulus across too many muscle fibers.

The MSF Exercise Practitioner must clearly communicate why repetition and consistency matter. At the same time, strategic programming can provide perceived variety without sacrificing fiber-specific stimulation. For example, performing leg press in one session and leg extension combined with abduction in another allows for different exercises while still targeting overlapping muscle fibers.

This approach maintains engagement while preserving the physiological benefits of frequency. There are plenty of examples of this strategy that can be further discussed with the Studio Leaders and MSF Corporate.

topics.title: Specificity
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 6 - Specificity.txt

blocks.text: Adaptations to exercise are specific to the type of stimulus the body encounters. This is known as the SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demand) principle in physical therapy and sports training. Resistance training not performed intensely enough, in a manner that imposes overload on the cardiovascular system, will not stimulate improvements in cardiovascular efficiency. Exercises performed for the muscles of the frontal thighs will not directly stimulate improvements in the strength of the shoulder muscles.

Exercise selection and method of performance should be specific to the types of adaptations desired. While a general program of high-intensity training produces overall improvements in all aspects of physical fitness, it is possible to alter the programs to target a particular muscle group or other aspects of fitness. And while strength remains our main focus, fatigue resistance or cardio can be emphasized by shortening rest periods between exercises. Or by running several compound movements sequentially in a workout. While this is not necessarily optimal for strength building, it is an example of specificity and how workout parameters can be adjusted to target different mechanisms.

topics.title: Individual Variability
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 7 - Individual Variability.txt

blocks.text: Why Individual Responses Differ
Individuals respond differently to exercise due to factors such as genetics, age, training history, motor control, and lifestyle.
While the same foundational exercise principles apply universally, their application must be adjusted to match the individual.
Some clients naturally demonstrate strong motor control and tolerate high levels of effort and mechanical tension.
Others may have limited coordination, lower tolerance for intensity, or heightened sensitivity to effort.
Because of this range, general exercise recommendations should always be treated as a starting point rather than a rigid prescription.
Application Within the MSF Model
The MSF methodology allows for precise adjustment of movement range, load, effort, and challenge without abandoning the core principles of high effort and mechanical tension.
Exercise Practitioners must be able to scale intensity appropriately while still preserving the integrity of the stimulus.
Customization does not mean reducing standards. It means meeting the client where they are while guiding them toward higher quality effort over time.
The goal is always to optimize internal stimulus while maintaining safety, confidence, and consistency.
The Role of the Exercise Practitioner
The ability to recognize individual differences and adapt sessions accordingly is a defining characteristic of a true professional.
This includes anticipating client needs, interpreting responses to training, and making real time adjustments without compromising outcomes.
Collaboration among trainers and consultation with MSF Corporate helps leverage collective experience and ensures consistency in decision making across studios.

topics.title: Productive Exercise - The Stimulating Reps Model
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy/Academy 3 - Basic Principles of Exercise/Academy - Basic Principles of Exercise 8 - Productive Exercise - The Stimulating Reps Model.txt

blocks.text: Overview

The Stimulating Reps model, developed by Chris Beardsley, explains which repetitions in a strength training set actually stimulate muscle growth and strength gains. Also recall that mechanical tension alone has been determined to be the primary driver of hypertrophy.
The key takeaway is simple but critical:
Only the final repetitions of a set, those performed with very high effort and involuntary slowing of the contraction velocity of the working muscles, create stimulative levels of mechanical tension.
These are referred to as stimulating, effective, or productive reps.

Importantly, this involuntary slowing is more of a requirement for those with more training experience. For true novice subjects, almost any level of intensity can be stimulative because it is a completely novel challenge.

To determine the contraction velocity of the working muscles, it is common practice to use the velocity of the movement/implement itself as a proxy. In our case at MSF, we would consider the movement arm of the machine, the experience of the instructor, and the subjective feelings of the client as to whether there is involuntary slowing present.
The Stimulating Reps Model helps define:
how hard a set must be
how close to failure a client must train
why some repetitions in a set may contribute little or no stimulus
What Is a Stimulating Rep?
A stimulating rep is a repetition performed when:
effort is very high, AND
the concentric phase involuntarily slows, despite the client attempting to maintain the same pace
A stimulating rep creates high levels of mechanical tension in the working muscles, which contributes to an adaptive response by the body in the form of increased muscle and/or strength.
Earlier repetitions, when the load moves smoothly and easily, do not produce sufficient mechanical tension, unless the subject is a relative beginner.
Why Involuntary Slowing Matters
At MSF, the single most important indicator of a stimulative effort is:
Involuntary slowing of the movement arm during the concentric phase
This slowing occurs because:
the subject is nearing their upper limit of motor unit recruitment (i.e. the total number of muscle fibers they can recruit or activate to contribute to a task)
this is effort dependant in that the higher the effort given, the higher the level of motor unit recruitment
the nervous system is unable to recruit additional, higher threshold motor units to continue the movement due to the limitations imposed by our maximum tolerable perception of effort
definition - a motor unit is a functional unit of muscle and consists of a motor neuron and all of the muscle fibers it controls
Importantly:
this slowing cannot be intentional for it to be stimulative (again, unless it is a beginner to resistance training)
it occurs as fatigue accumulates, especially near concentric failure
the subject must voluntarily decide to push/pull harder to maintain their pace
more simply stated, the involuntary slowing FORCES a higher level of effort from the subject to continue, which creates higher levels of mechanical tension
The closer a set is to concentric failure, the more likely the subject will experience involuntary slowing of the contraction.
Failure and the Stimulus
At MSF:
concentric failure is defined as “failure”, the inability to complete the full concentric phase despite maximal effort
However:
true failure itself is not necessarily required for strength or hypertrophy
however, training very close to failure is strongly encouraged to ensure a stimulus (especially for more experienced subjects)
most clients will stop well before true failure, even with encouragement
protective mechanisms naturally reduce effort as discomfort rises-this is known as the maximum tolerable perception of effort
the further a set is from true concentric failure, the less likely there will be involuntary slowing thereby reducing the potential for stimulus
For this reason:

Most clients should be encouraged to train to failure, or as close to it as safely possible, to ensure high enough levels of mechanical tension. This ability will be different for every client due to different levels of tolerance and skill and the instructor should be attuned to this level of individuality.
Strength training is a discipline that is influenced by skill:
tolerance to high levels of effort and uncomfortable sensations improves over time with more training
clients become more capable of reaching productive intensity with focused practice
mastery of execution is the ultimate form of long term progression
Load Selection and Repetition Range
Preferred Loading Strategy
MSF generally prefers:
moderate to heavy loads
lower repetition ranges
approximately 6 to 10 reps to failure or at least close
This approach:
allows clients to get closer to true failure with more focus
reduces excessive time, discomfort, and fatigue
improves the likelihood of involuntary slowing
increases mechanical tension on individual muscle fibers
Lighter Loads and Higher Reps
With lighter loads:
sets last longer
fatigue, discomfort, and unfavorable sensations increase
perceived effort rises disproportionately
clients often terminate sets well before a stimulus is achieved
Importantly, lighter loads are often still recommended for novice clients or the more intensity adverse to learn the attributes of proper execution.
Individual Variability
Some subjects are intensity adverse or may limited by injury:
heavier loads may not be appropriate
a moderate load may be used instead
a more therapeutic approach can be beneficial by avoiding failure or even involuntary slowing
Physiological Basis
This model is consistent with Henneman’s Size Principle:
lower threshold (slow twitch) motor units are recruited first
as force demands increase, higher threshold (fast twitch) motor units are recruited
high threshold motor units innervate (i.e. recruit) the muscle fibers with the greatest growth potential
High threshold motor units are fully recruited only when:
effort is very high, and
the active muscle fibers have reached their force producing limit
Involuntary slowing is the visible signal that these motor units are being recruited especially when the subject voluntarily increases their effort.
Tempo, Control, and Involuntary Slowing at MSF
MSF uses a voluntarily slow, controlled tempo:
6 to 10 seconds concentric
6 to 10 seconds eccentric
preference toward the faster end, approximately 6 seconds with the same pace being maintained on both phases
The purpose of this tempo is:
safety as the priority
ability to implement instruction
continuous force application
Key distinction:
the tempo is intentional at the beginning of the set
the slowing resulting from fatigue is not intentional
a set that begins intentionally slow EVENTUALLY becomes unintentionally slow if that set is taken close to concentric failure
Clients should be encouraged to:
Maintain the pace and form using as much effort and focus as possible.
Set Termination Guidelines
For most MSF clients:
sets should be taken at least close to concentric failure, or
terminated only when another repetition cannot be completed with proper execution
Exceptions include:
intensity adverse clients
injured or rehabbing clients
early stage trainees still developing skill and tolerance
for all of these situations, we are likely to use lighter loads with higher reps
Practitioner Observation and Instructional Cues
What the Practitioner Should Observe
slowing of the concentric phase
increasing effort required to maintain pace (accompanied by increasing respiration)
movement speed grinding to a halt near the end of the set
What the Practitioner Should Cue
encourage them to keep their pace and their form (posture)
“Keep pushing, don’t let it slow” or even “speed up!”
“This is the productive part of the set.”

Uncomfortable feelings/sensations are not necessarily stimulative and should not be emphasized or encouraged. These only act to increase the perception of effort and lead to the subject ending the set prematurely.
However, it is appropriate to acknowledge the client noticing the movement beginning to bog down.
This awareness helps the client:
increase effort
remain engaged and motivated
push closer to failure
Key Takeaways for the Exercise Practitioner
not all reps are equal (i.e. stimulative)
only reps performed with very high effort and involuntary slowing are likely to have stimulative levels of mechanical tension
involuntary slowing with increasing effort is the primary indicator of sufficient intensity
training close to failure is the most reliable way to ensure stimulus
heavier loads with fewer reps generally improve stimulus quality
pace is controlled intentionally out of concern for safety; slowing must be involuntary, especially for more experienced subjects
teaching effort and understanding the need to maintain pace when involuntary slowing begins are central to exercise execution at MSF
